source.title: Negotiate Anything
source.attribution: A Reborn guide in our own words, drawing on the Harvard Program on Negotiation, Hays and the classic Getting to Yes approach.
source.notes: Written by Reborn in our own words; no text copied. References: Harvard Program on Negotiation, Principled negotiation: focus on interests to create value, https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/negotiation-skills-daily/principled-negotiation-focus-interests-create-value/; Harvard Program on Negotiation, Translate your BATNA to the current deal, https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/batna/translate-your-batna-to-the-current-deal/; Harvard Program on Negotiation, Anchoring in negotiation, https://www.pon.harvard.edu/tag/anchoring-negotiation/; Harvard Program on Negotiation, Salary negotiations, https://www.pon.harvard.edu/daily/salary-negotiations/; Hays, How to ask for a pay rise, https://www.hays.com.au/career-advice/career-development/how-to-ask-for-a-pay-rise

cards.title: Negotiation is everyday problem-solving, not a fight
cards.body:
You negotiate far more than you think: with a landlord over repairs, a seller at the market, your family about chores, or an employer about pay. Many people avoid it because they picture a tense battle with a winner and a loser.

A better way to see it is as two people solving a shared problem. Each side wants something, and the task is to find an agreement that works well enough for both. That mindset lowers the temperature and usually leads to better deals.

Good negotiators are not the loudest or the toughest. They are the best prepared, the best listeners and the most willing to look for creative solutions. All of those can be learned.
cards.apply_it: List three things you could negotiate this month, big or small, such as a bill, a deadline or who does which chores.

quiz.question: What is a helpful way to think about negotiation?
options: A battle where one side must lose
Two sides solving a shared problem
A test of who can shout loudest
quiz.explanation: Seeing negotiation as joint problem-solving lowers tension and opens up better deals for both sides.

cards.title: Prepare before you say a word
cards.body:
Most of a negotiation is won or lost before it starts. Preparation gives you calm confidence and stops you agreeing to something you regret.

Work out what you want, and what you would ideally get, what is acceptable and what is not. Research fair prices or pay using adverts, price comparisons and people who know the market. Think about the other side too: what do they need, what pressures are they under and what alternatives do they have?

Then plan your opening, the questions you will ask and what you could offer in return. For example, before buying a used phone, check what similar models sell for, note any faults to point out and decide your top price.
cards.apply_it: For one upcoming negotiation, write down your ideal outcome, your acceptable outcome and one fact about the market price.

quiz.question: Which is part of good preparation for a negotiation?
options: Researching fair prices and thinking about the other side's needs
Thinking only about what you want
quiz.explanation: Knowing the market and understanding the other side's position gives you confidence and options.

cards.title: Know your walk-away point and your best alternative
cards.body:
Before any negotiation, ask: "What will I do if we can't agree?" Experts call your best answer your BATNA, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement. It might be another job offer, another seller or simply keeping things as they are.

Your BATNA sets your walk-away point. Any deal worse than your alternative is one you should turn down. Knowing this protects you from pressure, because you can calmly say no.

Compare alternatives fairly. A cheaper offer may hide weaker terms, so look at the whole package. And try to improve your BATNA before you start: getting a second quote or a second offer is one of the simplest ways to gain confidence and power.
cards.apply_it: For something you want to negotiate, write down what you will do if no deal is reached. Then find one way to make that alternative better.

quiz.question: What does BATNA stand for?
options: Bargain at the next available time
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement
quiz.explanation: Your BATNA is what you will do if no agreement is reached. It tells you when to walk away.

cards.title: Look behind positions to find the real interests
cards.body:
A position is what someone says they want: "I need a ten percent raise." An interest is why they want it: perhaps rising rent, feeling undervalued or wanting security. Positions often clash, but interests can usually be met in more than one way.

Imagine two siblings planning a parent's birthday. One insists on a restaurant, the other on a party at home. Talking reveals that one has no time to cook and the other worries about cost. An affordable restaurant solves both.

So don't argue over positions. Ask "Why is that important to you?" and share your own reasons. When you understand the needs on both sides, solutions appear that neither of you saw at first.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone makes a firm demand of you, ask gently "What matters most to you about that?" and listen to the answer.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a position and an interest?
options: A position is what someone asks for; an interest is why they want it
An interest is always about money
Positions are more important than interests
quiz.explanation: Understanding the reasons behind a demand opens up more ways to meet it.

cards.title: Aim high but stay reasonable, and use the first offer well
cards.body:
The first number mentioned in a negotiation often acts as an anchor: later offers tend to move around it. If you are well prepared, making the first offer lets you set that anchor in your favour.

Aim high, but keep it reasonable and backed by evidence, such as market prices or what similar people earn. An extreme opening can offend the other side and turn a friendly talk into hard haggling. Explaining your number helps: "Similar roles pay between X and Y, and with my experience I'm asking for Y."

If they anchor first, don't let it pull you. Calmly bring the conversation back to fair standards and your own research rather than bargaining only from their number.
cards.apply_it: Before your next negotiation, write down your opening offer and one piece of evidence you can use to explain it.

quiz.question: Why can making the first offer help you?
options: It can set an anchor that later offers move around
It means you never have to move
quiz.explanation: A well-researched first offer anchors the talk in your favour, as long as it is reasonable.

cards.title: Listen more than you talk, and ask open questions
cards.body:
Information is power in a negotiation, and you gain it by listening. The more you understand what the other side needs, fears and values, the easier it is to find a deal they will accept.

Ask open questions that can't be answered with yes or no: "What would make this work for you?" "What's driving the deadline?" "How did you arrive at that price?" Then really listen, rather than planning your next point.

Sum up what you heard: "So the price matters less than getting it delivered this week?" This shows respect, checks you understood and often reveals room to agree. People also become more flexible when they feel truly heard.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation where you want something, ask at least two open questions before you state your own view.

quiz.question: Which is an open question?
options: What would make this work for you?
quiz.explanation: Open questions invite people to explain, which gives you useful information.

cards.title: Let silence do some of the work
cards.body:
Many people find silence uncomfortable and rush to fill it, often by lowering their price or adding a concession they didn't need to give. You can use this calmly to your advantage, and avoid falling for it yourself.

After you make an offer, stop talking. Don't explain it three times or apologise for it. Let the other person respond. When they make an offer, you can pause, look thoughtful and take a few seconds before replying. Often they will add something to fill the gap.

Patience in general is powerful. You don't have to decide on the spot. Saying "Let me think about that and come back to you tomorrow" gives you time to check the details.
cards.apply_it: Next time you make a request or offer, say it once clearly and then count silently to five before speaking again.

quiz.question: What should you do right after making an offer?
options: Stop talking and let the other person respond
quiz.explanation: Staying quiet gives the other side space to respond and stops you giving away value by nervously filling the gap.

cards.title: Trade, don't just concede
cards.body:
If you give something away for nothing, the other side learns that pushing works and will push again. Instead, make every concession a trade: "If I do this, can you do that?"

For example, when buying furniture you might say, "I can pay today in full if you include free delivery." At work: "I can take on the extra project if we push back the other deadline." Both sides get something they value.

Go into a negotiation knowing which things matter a lot to you and which matter less. Things that are cheap for you but valuable to them, like flexibility on timing, are perfect to trade. Move in smaller steps as you go, which signals you are nearing your limit.
cards.apply_it: List two things you could offer in your next negotiation that cost you little but might matter to the other side.

quiz.question: What does "trade, don't concede" mean?
options: Ask for something in return whenever you give something
Give everything away to be liked
quiz.explanation: Linking each concession to something in return keeps the deal balanced and stops endless pushing.

cards.title: Look for a win-win by widening the options
cards.body:
Many negotiations get stuck because both sides fight over a single thing, usually money. You can often unlock a deal by adding more items to the table and brainstorming options before deciding.

In a job offer, that might mean training, flexible hours, a start date or a pay review after six months. When renting a flat, it could be a longer contract in exchange for a lower rent, or doing some repairs yourself.

When you disagree, suggest a fair, outside standard you can both accept, like market prices or an independent quote. This turns a contest of wills into a shared search for what is fair, and it protects the relationship for next time.
cards.apply_it: For something you want to negotiate, brainstorm at least four different things that could be part of the deal, not just the price.

quiz.question: How can you get past a deadlock over a single number?
options: Add more items to the deal and agree on fair outside standards
quiz.explanation: More options and shared standards create room for both sides to gain.

cards.title: Put the agreement in writing
cards.body:
A deal that is only spoken can be remembered differently by each side, especially weeks later. Once you reach agreement, write it down.

For anything important, such as a job offer, a rental, a loan to a friend or a large purchase, ask for or send a written summary. Include who will do what, by when, how much, and what happens if something goes wrong. An email is often enough: "Thanks for today. To confirm, we agreed..."

Read the written version carefully before signing or accepting, and question anything that differs from what you discussed. This simple step prevents most misunderstandings and protects good relationships as well as your money.
cards.apply_it: After your next agreement with someone, send a short message confirming the key points: what, who, how much and by when.

quiz.question: Why should you put an agreement in writing?
options: To prevent different memories of what was agreed
To show you don't trust the other person
quiz.explanation: A written summary prevents misunderstandings and gives both sides something clear to refer back to.

cards.title: Negotiate your salary with evidence and courtesy
cards.body:
Salary is one of the most valuable things you will ever negotiate, because each raise affects every future one. Yet many people accept the first offer out of fear.

Research the usual pay range for the role and location. When an offer comes, thank them warmly, show enthusiasm for the job and ask for time to consider it. Then make a polite, specific counter-offer backed by your research and the value you bring.

If they can't move on pay, ask about other things: a signing bonus, extra leave, training, flexible working or a review in six months. Stay friendly throughout. You will be working with these people, and a respectful negotiation often raises their opinion of you.
cards.apply_it: Find the typical pay range for your current or next role from at least three sources, and write down a figure you could confidently ask for.

quiz.question: If an employer can't raise the salary, what can you do?
options: Threaten to post about it online
Ask about other benefits like training, leave or an early pay review
quiz.explanation: Other parts of the package can add real value when the base pay is fixed.

cards.title: Negotiate everyday prices and bills politely
cards.body:
You can negotiate much more than people think: phone and internet bills, rent, repairs, car prices and market goods. In many places, bargaining at markets is expected, while elsewhere it is about asking politely for a better deal.

Check what competitors charge first. Then ask simply: "Is that the best price you can do?" or "I've seen this cheaper elsewhere; can you match it?" With service providers, ask for the customer retention team and mention you are thinking of leaving.

Be friendly, be ready to walk away and don't be embarrassed by a no. The worst outcome is usually that you pay what you would have paid anyway. Over a year, a few polite questions can save a surprising amount.
cards.apply_it: Choose one regular bill. Check a competitor's price, then contact your provider and politely ask if they can offer a better deal.

quiz.question: What is usually the worst outcome of politely asking for a better price?
options: You pay what you would have paid anyway
The seller refuses to ever serve you again
quiz.explanation: A polite request carries little risk, which is why it is worth asking.
